q-328705.name: Question 1
q-328705.problem:
Consider a function $f(t)$ such that its Laplace transform is $L\{f(t)\}=F(s)$ for $s>{s}_{0}.$ Suppose we wish to find $L\{{e}^{2t}f(t)\}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below. By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write 

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{2t}f(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-1}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={{field-3}}\,\text{for}\,{{field-4}}.\end{aligned}
$$
q-328705.worked_solution:
Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{2t}f(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{2t}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-2)t}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t,$ where $s>{s}_{0}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-2)t}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t=F(s-2),
$$

where 

$$
s-2>{s}_{0}\,⇒\,s>{s}_{0}+2.
$$

q-332063.name: Question 2
q-332063.problem: Consider a function $f(t)$ for which the Laplace transform is $L\{f(t)\}=F(s).$ How can we obtain the graph of $L\{{e}^{8t}f(t)\}$ from the graph of $F(s)?$
q-332063.worked_solution:
The first shifting theorem states that if
$L\{f(t)\}=F(s),$
then
$L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a).$

This implies that multiplying a function $f(t)$ by ${e}^{at}$ shifts the corresponding Laplace transform horizontally along the $s$-axis.

- If $a>0,$ the graph of $F(s)$ shifts to the right.

- If $a<0,$ the graph of $F(s)$ shifts to the left.

In our case, to get the graph of $L\{{e}^{8t}f(t)\},$ we must shift the graph of $F(s)$ by $8$ units to the right.

Consider a function f(t) for which the Laplace transform is L{f(t)}=F(s). How can we obtain the graph of L{e8tf(t)} from the graph of F(s)?

a
Shift the graph of F(s) by 8 units to the right.
b
Scale the graph of F(s) by a scale factor of 8 horizontally.
c
The Laplace transform is unchanged.
d
Scale the graph of F(s) by a scale factor of 8 vertically.
e
Shift the graph of F(s) by 8 units to the left.
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The first shifting theorem states that if L{f(t)}=F(s), then L{eatf(t)}=F(s−a).

This implies that multiplying a function f(t) by eat shifts the corresponding Laplace transform horizontally along the s-axis.

  • If a>0, the graph of F(s) shifts to the right.

  • If a<0, the graph of F(s) shifts to the left.

In our case, to get the graph of L{e8tf(t)}, we must shift the graph of F(s) by 8 units to the right.

q-332127.name: Question 4
q-332127.problem:
Given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{n}\} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}, &  & s>0,\end{aligned}
$$

use linearity of Laplace transforms and the first shifting theorem to find the Laplace transform of $f(t)=6t+4{t}^{3}{e}^{2t}$ for $s>2.$
q-332127.worked_solution:
First, we apply the linearity properties of Laplace transforms:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =L\{6t+4{t}^{3}{e}^{2t}\} \\  & =L\{6t\}+L\{4{t}^{3}{e}^{2t}\} \\  & =6L\{t\}+4L\{{t}^{3}{e}^{2t}\}\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that, for $s>0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{n}\} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{t\} & =\frac{1}{{s}^{2}} \\ L\{{t}^{3}\} & =\frac{6}{{s}^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

The first shifting theorem states that if $L\{f(t)\}=F(s),$ then $L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a).$ Therefore,

$$
L\{{t}^{3}{e}^{2t}\}=\frac{6}{(s-2)^{4}}.
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =6L\{t\}+4L\{{t}^{3}{e}^{2t}\} \\  & =6\cdot \frac{1}{{s}^{2}}+4\cdot \frac{6}{(s-2)^{4}} \\  & =\frac{6}{{s}^{2}}+\frac{24}{(s-2)^{4}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This transform is valid for $s>2.$

Given that L{tn}=n!sn+1,s>0, use linearity of Laplace transforms and the first shifting theorem to find the Laplace transform of f(t)=6t+4t3e2t for s>2.

a
1s2+6(s−2)4
b
6s2+24(s−2)4
c
3s2+12(s−2)4
d
6s2+4(s−2)3
e
6s3+24(s−2)4
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we apply the linearity properties of Laplace transforms:

L{f(t)}=L{6t+4t3e2t}=L{6t}+L{4t3e2t}=6L{t}+4L{t3e2t}

We are given that, for s>0, L{tn}=n!sn+1.

Therefore, we have the following: L{t}=1s2L{t3}=6s4

The first shifting theorem states that if L{f(t)}=F(s), then L{eatf(t)}=F(s−a). Therefore, L{t3e2t}=6(s−2)4.

Therefore, the Laplace transform of f(t) is

L{f(t)}=6L{t}+4L{t3e2t}=6⋅1s2+4⋅6(s−2)4=6s2+24(s−2)4.

This transform is valid for s>2.
